claims.text: H13 steel or similar tool-steel components can possess microstructural features that promote hot cracking during fusion-welding repair.
Laser cladding an AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA coating onto a damaged component can provide a localized surface repair.
Additional alloying elements can tailor the thermal expansion and phase stability of an AlCoCrFeNi-based coating.
High-energy-density laser processing with rapid cooling produces low dilution and good metallurgical bonding.
Laser cladding produces a refined, dense, low-dilution, metallurgically bonded HEA coating.
The refined, low-dilution coating minimizes residual thermal stresses.
Localized melting and rapid solidification during laser cladding promote a fine-grained coating.
The fine-grained coating increases surface hardness.
The laser-clad microstructure and reduced thermal stresses lower the propensity for hot cracking.
HEA cocktail effects and lattice distortion enhance wear resistance.
HEA cocktail effects and lattice distortion enhance corrosion resistance.
HEA cocktail effects and lattice distortion enhance thermal stability.
The laser-clad HEA coating will increase surface hardness by approximately 50–100 HV relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The coating will reduce crack initiation during cyclic thermal loading relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The coating will reduce wear rate relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The coating will improve passivation behavior relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs are prone to hot cracking because of their extensive heating cycles.
The proposed coating is expected to perform under thermal cycling to approximately 800 °C, wear, and corrosive exposure.
